You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: 【Bitget US Stock Weekly Recap】Inflation cools more than expected + Banks & ASML & TSMC deliver a triple beat Traders first breathed a sigh of relief, then got spooked by Capex.

TEXT:
This week the market delivered a classic V-shaped rebound. On Monday, the re-escalation of the US-Iran conflict combined with a sharp drop in SK Hynix shares sent the Nasdaq down as much as 1.6%. Then came the dual CPI/PPI prints that came in well below expectations, a clean sweep of beats from the major banks, ASML ’s significant full-year guidance raise, and TSMC ’s record gross margin and net profit. Sentiment recovered quickly.
However, on Thursday TSMC paired its strong results with a sharp upward revision of capital expenditure to $60–64 billion. Chip stocks sold off collectively and the market once again wrestled with the question: “Is AI spending getting too aggressive?”
As of Thursday’s close, the S&P 500 was still up roughly +1.2% for the week, the Nasdaq about +1.5%, and the Dow closed slightly higher. The AI hardware thesis was reaffirmed, but Capex sensitivity under elevated valuations has clearly risen.
1. Macro, Black Swan, Geopolitics & Liquidity Review
Three factors dominated positioning this week:
1. Inflation cooled sharply and unexpectedly June CPI fell 0.4% month-over-month (vs. –0.2% expected), the largest monthly decline since April 2020, and rose 3.5% year-over-year (vs. 3.8% expected). Core CPI was flat month-over-month and only +2.6% year-over-year. PPI declined 0.3% month-over-month and rose 5.5% year-over-year (well below the 6.2% consensus). Energy prices were the main driver. The data effectively extinguished July rate-hike expectations. The 10-year Treasury yield pulled back toward 4.55%, giving risk assets room to breathe.
2. US-Iran conflict re-ignited (the biggest black swan) President Trump declared the earlier ceasefire “over.” US strikes continued and Hormuz risks returned. Brent crude jumped above $83 on Monday, contributing to the sharp equity sell-off. Later mediation headlines helped oil partially retrace to the $79–80 range, and the market began to digest the risk.
3. Rapid rotation in liquidity and risk appetite After the inflation data, capital rotated out of defensive sectors back into growth and semiconductors. However, TSMC’s large Capex raise on Thursday triggered profit-taking in chip stocks, amplifying volatility in leveraged positions.
Summary of price action Monday: S&P 500 –0.8% to 7,515, Nasdaq –1.6%. Wednesday: S&P 500 recovered to 7,572, Nasdaq to 26,269. Thursday: Chip stocks dragged the indices, giving back some of the gains, but the week still closed positive overall.
2. Earnings Highlights – Banks + ASML + TSMC
Earnings season truly kicked off this week, and three sectors delivered clear signals:
1. Banks delivered a perfect start (July 14–15) JPMorgan reported record net income of $21.2 billion (EPS $7.70, adjusted EPS $6.14, a significant beat). Investment banking and trading revenues were exceptionally strong. Bank of America, Citigroup , Wells Fargo, and Goldman Sachs all beat expectations, with trading and investment banking fees surging (including contributions linked to SpaceX activity). The strength in banks signaled that “money is moving and volatility is profitable,” which directly lifted risk appetite.
2. Semiconductor equipment leader ASML (July 15) Net sales came in at €9.3 billion (well above the €8.4–9.0 billion guidance), gross margin 54.0%, net income €2.9 billion, EPS €7.59. More importantly, the company sharply raised full-year guidance to €43–45 billion (from the previous €36–40 billion range) and guided Q3 net sales to €11.0–12.0 billion. CEO explicitly stated that AI demand remains extremely strong and Installed Base Management outperformed. The stock rose as much as ~8% intraday and closed up about 3%, igniting the entire AI equipment complex.
3. TSMC (July 16) Q2 revenue $40.2 billion (at the high end of guidance), gross margin 67.7% (vs. 65.5–67.5% guidance, a clear beat), and record net profit of approximately $22.0 billion (+77.4% YoY). Q3 revenue guidance $44.6–45.8 billion. Full-year revenue growth was raised to “slightly above 40%” (from “above 30%”). Capex was significantly increased to $60–64 billion (from $52–56 billion), and the company announced an additional $10 billion investment in Arizona.
The market reaction was classic “sell the news”: TSM fell after hours, dragging NVIDIA , Micron, SK Hynix and other chip names lower on Thursday. Traders simultaneously acknowledged the AI super-cycle while worrying that “spending is too aggressive and the payback period is lengthening.”
Banks proved economic resilience; ASML and TSMC together confirmed that AI hardware demand is still accelerating — this was the core fundamental signal of the week.
3. Trader Sentiment Resonance
Sentiment this week was extreme and authentic:
On Monday many were waiting for a pullback to add to AI positions. Instead, geopolitics plus the SK Hynix plunge forced high-leverage longs to stop out, and the market briefly filled with “is the AI bubble about to burst?” panic.
The CPI print immediately squeezed shorts and capital rotated back in. After ASML raised guidance, chat rooms flipped to “AI is still racing ahead.”
After TSMC’s report on Thursday, sentiment split again. The fundamental story remains intact, but the large Capex increase prompted some funds to take profits. The current consensus is clear: inflation gave the market a break, the AI hardware thesis has been double-confirmed, and the trade can continue — but under high valuations, sensitivity to capital spending has increased. Do not run full position sizes. Defensive names enjoyed a brief moment of favor before being discarded again. Volatility subsided and sentiment shifted from panic toward “cautiously optimistic + high-beta trading.”
4. Next Week’s Key Calendar (Beijing Time )
The data calendar is relatively light. Focus remains on earnings, geopolitics, and the pre-FOMC positioning window:
July 20: Leading Economic Index
July 21–22: Industrial and auto names including 3M and General Motors
July 23: Initial jobless claims
Ongoing: US-Iran negotiation updates, oil price swings, additional tech and consumer earnings
Key preview: July 28–29 FOMC meeting (an important meeting under new Chair Kevin Warsh)
5. Trading Priority for Next Week
Prioritize high-beta AI semiconductor names while keeping a modest energy/ gold hedge and watching pre-FOMC position adjustments.
Biggest takeaway of the week Cooling inflation + strong banks + dual confirmation from ASML and TSMC of the AI super-cycle gave the market a clear “continue” signal. Geopolitics remains the largest wildcard, and Thursday’s Capex reaction reminded everyone that in a high-valuation environment, even good news can be offset by concerns about “spending too much.”
Trading suggestion for next week Favor long exposure in high-elasticity AI hardware names, but strictly control overall position size. Do not put all chips on one side of the table. Remember — no matter how good the data looks, a sudden Hormuz disruption or another Capex surprise can reverse sentiment in an instant.
